items.readable_text:
Content:
Another way of describing a set is to use a so-called conditional definition.

Content:
Consider the following set:

Content:
[MATH: A = \big\{n \in \mathbb{Z}: |3n-1|=2 \big\}]

Content:
This notation tells us that the elements of [MATH: A] are the integers [MATH: (n\in\mathbb Z)] that satisfy the absolute value equation

Content:
[MATH: |3n-1| = 2.]

Content:
To list the elements of this set, we start by solving this equation:

Content:
[MATH: |3n − 1||= 2; 3n − 1|= ± 2; 3n|= 1 ± 2; n|= (1 ± 2)/(3)]
So, the solutions to our equation are [MATH: n=1] and [MATH: n=-\dfrac13.]

Content:
We now inspect each solution to see which of them (if any) are elements of [MATH: A{:}]

Content:
- The solution [MATH: n=1] is an integer. Hence, this solution is a member of [MATH: A.]
- The solution [MATH: n=-\dfrac13] is not an integer. Hence, this solution is not a member of [MATH: A.]

Content:
Therefore, the set [MATH: A] contains only one element.

Content:
Finally, listing all elements of [MATH: A,] we have
[MATH: A = \{1\}.]

sections.normalized_html: Note the following:
sections.readable_text: Note the following:

sections.normalized_html:
• Under this definition, [MATH: n\in\mathbb Z] describes the universal set for the type of mathematical object we're considering. In this case, the universal set is the set of integers.

  • The condition [MATH: |3n-1| = 2] is a predicate that defines the set's internal logic. Therefore, [MATH: A] is the set of integers that give a true statement when substituted into the equation [MATH: |3n-1| = 2.]

  • Note that [MATH: A] itself is not a predicate but a set; therefore, it does not have a truth value.

  • When a set is written using a conditional definition, the symbol "[MATH: :]" is read as "such that." So, in words, we can describe the set [MATH: A] as follows:

    [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: A] is the set of integers [MATH: n] such that [MATH: |3n-1| = 2.]

  • The variable [MATH: n] is a dummy variable. Its purpose is to describe the logic behind the set's definition and can be replaced with any other variable.

  • An alternative to the "conditional definition of a set" terminology is to say the set is written using set-builder notation.

  • Instead of using a "[MATH: :]" symbol to separate the universal set from its predicate, it's common to use the "[MATH: |]" symbol, as follows: [MATH: A = \big\{n \in \mathbb{Z}\:\mid\:\ |3n-1|=2 \big\}]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Another way of describing a set is to use a so-called conditional definition.

Content:
Consider the following set:

Content:
[MATH: A = \big\{n \in \mathbb{Z}: |3n-1|=2 \big\}]

Content:
This notation tells us that the elements of [MATH: A] are the integers [MATH: (n\in\mathbb Z)] that satisfy the absolute value equation

Content:
[MATH: |3n-1| = 2.]

Content:
To list the elements of this set, we start by solving this equation:

Content:
[MATH: |3n − 1||= 2; 3n − 1|= ± 2; 3n|= 1 ± 2; n|= (1 ± 2)/(3)]
So, the solutions to our equation are [MATH: n=1] and [MATH: n=-\dfrac13.]

Content:
We now inspect each solution to see which of them (if any) are elements of [MATH: A{:}]

Content:
- The solution [MATH: n=1] is an integer. Hence, this solution is a member of [MATH: A.]
- The solution [MATH: n=-\dfrac13] is not an integer. Hence, this solution is not a member of [MATH: A.]

Content:
Therefore, the set [MATH: A] contains only one element.

Content:
Finally, listing all elements of [MATH: A,] we have
[MATH: A = \{1\}.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Some Comments

Content:
Let's go back to our set, written using a conditional definition:

Content:
[MATH: A = \big\{n \in \mathbb{Z}: |3n-1|=2 \big\}]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Under this definition, [MATH: n\in\mathbb Z] describes the universal set for the type of mathematical object we're considering. In this case, the universal set is the set of integers.
- The condition [MATH: |3n-1| = 2] is a predicate that defines the set's internal logic. Therefore, [MATH: A] is the set of integers that give a true statement when substituted into the equation [MATH: |3n-1| = 2.]
- Note that [MATH: A] itself is not a predicate but a set; therefore, it does not have a truth value.
- When a set is written using a conditional definition, the symbol "[MATH: :]" is read as "such that." So, in words, we can describe the set [MATH: A] as follows:

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: A] is the set of integers [MATH: n] such that [MATH: |3n-1| = 2.]
- The variable [MATH: n] is a dummy variable. Its purpose is to describe the logic behind the set's definition and can be replaced with any other variable.
- An alternative to the "conditional definition of a set" terminology is to say the set is written using set-builder notation.
- Instead of using a "[MATH: :]" symbol to separate the universal set from its predicate, it's common to use the "[MATH: |]" symbol, as follows:
[MATH: A = \big\{n \in \mathbb{Z}\:\mid\:\ |3n-1|=2 \big\}]

---
